4809.tone: Three lexical tones on every main syllable: low Tone 1, checked Tone 2 (on checked/stopped syllables), falling Tone 3; voice quality is a non-distinctive accompaniment of tone (p. 61). Presyllables are toneless and their vowel is non-contrastive, so they are transcribed /C./ (p. 56). Tone is 'closely linked with syllable structure' (p. 61); Hall 2014 JSEALS 7 argues the indigenous tones would be largely predictable from syllable structure and vowel length were it not for Tai Lue loans. Nothing on stress or accent beyond the p. 60 remark; 'accent marks' in Hall 2014 refers to tone diacritics.

4809.sec_quote: The presyllable in Muak Sa-aak has no contrast in the tone or the vowel. It serves essentially to place an open transition between consonants which are not permitted as consonant clusters. Therefore although the language is sesquisyllabic, it is actually very close to being monosyllabic. The word structure may be summarized as (C.).C(C)V(C)T.

4813.heavy: 'groupe lourd... c'est-à-dire V̄C ou VCC': a long vowel followed by a consonant, or a short vowel followed by two consonants. Stated as a segmental sequence, not a syllable type: the long vowel plus the following onset counts (dafā́tər, lā́bisah), as does a closed syllable plus the following onset (baqárti, tegámmaʿū); word-final CVC (rúkab) and word-final CV̄ (kátabū) are not heavy; word-final CV̄C (buṭū́n, lābᵊsā́t) is heavy.
4813.dflt: first syllable of the word: rúkab 'knees', kátabū 'they wrote', báqarah 'a cow'
4813.prule: Stress falls on the rightmost heavy sequence in the word, where heavy = V̄C (long vowel followed by a consonant) or VCC (short vowel followed by two consonants), counting from the end of the word; if the word contains no such sequence, stress falls on the first syllable. A word-final CVC (rúkab) or word-final long vowel (kátabū) does not count as heavy.

4815.heavy: 'долгий гласный' — a syllable with a long vowel (ā ī ē ō ū); examples cover word-final CVVC (riǧǧāl, giddām, ibʿīr, tišrabīn, mitmūt, laḳēt, šaddēt; also Dž. eyṣāb, iyṣāb), word-final CVV(ʰ) (Ar. manāʰ) — the last three printed without a stress mark, i.e. stressed on the final long vowel by the convention — and non-final CVV (madīna, sakkīna, ilēha). Closed syllables with short vowels are not said to be heavy (minḥásad / mínḥasad).
4815.dflt: Unstated as a general rule. Partial evidence only: disyllabic verbs initial (ḥásad, ḥáfar, ṭábaḥ); VII/VIII imperfects second syllable in Arab-khana (minḥásad) but first syllable in Jogari (mínḥasad); Ar. éyṣab, íyṣab (initial; both variants printed with the acute) and Dž. mánaʰ (initial) — whereas Dž. eyṣāb, iyṣāb and Ar. manāʰ have a final long vowel and so fall under the long-vowel rule, not the light-only default; forms with the 3f.sg. suffix -ha 'always on the penult' (Vinnikov 1962 s.v. -ha: našára, malbáḳa, maṭbáḫa, nafáza, ḳadíra, ḳabíra); final short vowel stressed in loanwords and under clash.
4815.prule: Stress falls on the syllable containing a long vowel whenever the word has one, in any position (final riǧǧāl, giddām, tišrabīn, mitmūt; non-final madīna, sakkīna, ilēha); the author calls this the 'original' (Old Arabic) character of stress. Words with two long vowels are 'extremely rare' and their stress is marked case by case. For words with no long vowel the note gives no general rule.
4815.srule: Not mentioned in Vinnikov 1969, preface pp. 3-11 (stress treated on p. 5 'Ударение' and pp. 10-11 transcription note), nor in the parallel notes Vinnikov 1962 pp. 5-6 and 1949 p. 121 n. 1: one stress per word (on the long vowel when there is one) and one stress per tied word group; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described.

4818.heavy: Not rime weight: the attracting property is vowel height/sonority. 'it occurs on an earlier syllable if that syllable's vowel is lower than the vowel(s) of any succeeding syllables' (a lowest, e/o mid, i/u high; the vowel system is i e a o u). 4818.prule: Primary stress is fully predictable ('redundant'): by default it falls on the final syllable of the phonological word (root plus affixes, clitics and the formative -a- excluded), but it falls on an earlier syllable whose vowel is lower (a < e,o < i,u in height) than the vowel(s) of every following syllable. Examples: [ta'man], [u'sol], [ifu'no], [tigi'o] (final); ['nanun], ['ŋasol], ['ayan], ['mra.mor]/[mu.'ra.mor], [ka.'na.o.ˌrig], [ku.ˌma.ti.'a.o] (non-final). tn.translation: On tone. Seligmann marked stress accents here and there. I myself tried to record the musical tones. Probably both stress accents and musical tones are present in the language. The pitches seem to change little within the sentence. Klingenheben has the following examples: gya's gye sa re gya dok 'the dog's head is small'. Here gya's simply has high tone, which otherwise is noted with high-low (falling) tone by Klg. and me. 4824.prule: Word stress on the last non-enclitic syllable of the word (source's formulation, all three Iranian Taleshi dialects: Anbarani, Asalemi, Masali); quantity-insensitive. 4829.dq: In Tanchangya, there are several pairs of homophonous words, whose precise meanings are conveyed by the speaker using a two-way tonal contrast.
4829.dloc: ch. 2 'Ethno-linguistics', sec. 2.6 'Language', p. 71; sec. 2.6.2 'Phonology', pp. 74-80, tone paragraph and minimal-pair table p. 79; vowel-length remark p. 74; glottal-stop / low-fall remark p. 76
4829.heavy: not applicable (no stress rule); on length the source says (p. 74) 'Vowel lengthening is not distinctive of Tanchangya but in some open monosyllables, vowels are articulated long.'
4829.prule: No word-stress rule is stated anywhere in the source. What it reports is a two-way lexical tone contrast, low level vs low fall, distinguishing otherwise homophonous words (za 'go' low level vs za 'jungle' low fall; asi 'smile' low fall vs asi 'eighty' low level; bisi 'seed' low level vs bisi 'mongoose' low fall), which the author himself calls preliminary; a low-fall tone is also said to be left behind where an Indo-Aryan h- > glottal stop has been elided (p. 76).
4829.srule: Not mentioned in Debnath 2008, sec. 2.6-2.6.2 (pp. 71, 74-80, read in full): the source has no statement on word stress at all, primary or secondary; it reports only a preliminary two-way tone contrast.

[p.79] In Tanchangya, there are several pairs of homophonous words, whose precise meanings are conveyed by the speaker using a two-way…
4829.loc: ch. 2 'Ethno-linguistics', sec. 2.6 'Language', p. 71; sec. 2.6.2 'Phonology', pp. 74-80, tone paragraph and minimal-pair table p. 79; vowel-length remark p. 74; glottal-stop / low-fall remark p. 76
4829.idn: Tanchangya as spoken in the Chittagong Hill Tracts (Bangladesh), CADC (Chakma Autonomous District Council, Mizoram), South Tripura and North Arakan (Sittwe), with kinship-based (gosa) sub-dialects: Karwa gosa (KG), Muo gosa (MuG), Daingnya gosa (DG), Melong gosa (MeG), Mongla gosa (MoG), Langbasa (LB), Angya gosa…
4829.exq_: But these findings are only preliminary and require extensive study to arrive at definite conclusions.
4829.tone: The source (an ethnographer's sketch, not a phonological study) states 'occurrence of tone contrasts with changes in laryngeal and supra-laryngeal settings of phonemes' (p. 71) and 'a two-way tonal contrast' between low level and low fall on 'several pairs of homophonous words' (p. 79, table of four minimal pairs with Chakma and Bengali cognates); tone shapes are said to be affected by voice quality and consonant elision, and IA h- > glottal stop, elided in most gosa sub-dialects, leaves 'a low-fall tone' in its place (p. 76); the orthography is said to carry a low-fall tone character and possibly an older mid-level tone marker (pp. 74, 79). The author flags all of this as preliminary. Stress, accent and prominence are not discussed in the source (its only use of the word 'accent', p. 15, is in a quoted remark about the Mru, a different people). Sister language Chakma (chak1266) is analysed by Huziwara 2019 as a pitch-accent system with non-distinctive stress; that analysis is not transferable to Tanchangya without a source.

4834.prule: No positional rule in the open text: accent is lexically contrastive (minimal pair díka 'he laughs' vs di-ká 'he sees'), realised as a pitch-type accent; each phonological word carries one primary stress, and long and nasal vowels are always stressed. The placement section (§2.3, pp. 37-39; §2.4.1 p. 40 'Primary stress and prosodic classes of morphemes') is paywalled; its content is known only second-hand (Wikipedia paraphrase of pp. 37-39): primary stress on one of the last three syllables, penultimate most common in monomorphemic words (dúpu), antepenultimate (képira) and final (yapuratú) also occur; roots carry underlying stress, prefixes are unstressed, suffixes are lexically stressed or unstressed.
4834.srule: Secondary stress falls on enclitics: every enclitic obligatorily carries a secondary stress (`), unlike suffixes, which do not (grammar p. xvii; Tariana Texts 1999 p. 17). 4834.tone: Not a tone language. The author calls the accent 'contrastive, and of a pitch type' (grammar p. 1), 'distinctive and of pitch type' (Encyclopedia typescript p. 5), 'contrastif... et tonal' (Le tariana p. 4), attributing the pitch realisation to Tucano influence; her 1999 areal chapter (Dixon & Aikhenvald, The Amazonian Languages, pp. 405-407) lists Tariana among the Vaupés languages with pitch accent (a low-high distinction). The grammar nevertheless analyses it as primary vs secondary STRESS on a lexically specified syllable, with vowel reduction of unstressed syllables (§2.3.5) — a stress-accent whose main correlate is pitch. Coded lexical (contrastive, lexically specified accent); tone or pitch accent is the literal alternative mapping if the editor wants 'pitch type' taken as the system type.

dfl.note: SECOND-HAND ONLY (Wikipedia paraphrase of grammar p. 38): primary stress within the last three syllables, penultimate most common in monomorphemic words; antepenultimate and final also occur. No first-hand open page names a default.
dfl.q: Otherwise, primary stress may fall on the last three syllables. Penultimate stress in most common in monomorphemic words (e.g. dúpu "a lizard"), but antepenultimate (e.g. képira "bird") and final stress (e.g. yapuratú "long flute used at ritual offering") also occurs.
